          The Country Cramming for the AI Revolution
            In China, the fear of getting left behind has created a powerful new prosperity gospel.
            

            
            
            By 
        Afra Wang,
          a journalist covering AI in Silicon Valley and China
          
      

              
          
        
      
          
            
              
                    Oct. 15, 2026
              
            
            
                Illustration: Alberto Miranda
            
             
                
                  
                    
  


                  
                
                
                  Save this article to read it later.

In May, I sat in a living room on the fringes of Hangzhou, one of the most technologically advanced cities in China and home to Alibaba, Unitree, and DeepSeek. In many ways, the party that was about to start resembled one that you’d find in any coastal metropolis: ten professionals in their 20s padding barefoot across the carpet, snacks on the dining table. Only the laptops scattered across the floor and couch suggested this was a different type of social gathering, one that has grown common in the past three years in China’s towns and cities. Our host, KC, has gathered a small circle of friends to learn AI.

KC’s face is still marked with acne; he is tall and thin, barely past 20, and already a vibe coder of some local fame. Today he’ll teach others how to use Codex and Figma to quickly build websites, Electron desktop apps, install packages — but the first step is teaching everyone to “put up the ladder,” the euphemism for deploying VPNs and relays that bypass OpenAI’s geo-block. Like any self-organized class, it doesn’t really begin until nearly two hours in. Only as the sky darkens do people settle down, grow patient, and start the class.

The demographic of the room is young, hungry, yet refusing to join or be excluded from the rat race of big tech — they self-identify as engineers, designers, influencers, or, to use a more fashionable term, one-person companies (OPCs). They are members of a social species typical of a generation facing 18.9 percent unemployment, astronomical real-estate prices in big cities, and a battered post-COVID economy, which a friend describes as petit bourgeois, overeducated, downwardly mobile young people who can just barely make the rent. A few years ago, low-cost towns like Liangzhu (where KC lives), Dali, and Anji started actively courting digital nomads and vibe coders like them. Amid government campaigns and a stream of social-media posts, young people started washing up there, hoping that learning AI while keeping their expenses low might change something.

During the self-introduction session, one woman mentions, a little shyly, her old life at Tencent — which she had disliked so much that she quit to explore “the many ways of not going to work.” Another, with long black hair, introduces herself as a novelist serializing a long book on Jinjiang Literature City, China’s biggest women-focused web-fiction platform. A third says she used to work in fashion and now runs an “aesthetics and shopping-companion” business with a friend and does self-media and AI projects on the side. They are all convinced that AI could empower their work.

Since ChatGPT, a new consensus has hardened across China’s tech industry: AI is the next mobile internet. On the surface, the country seems to have arrived at a near-universal embrace of new technology. Xi Jinping has described AI as an essential engine for China’s “new quality productive forces.” From a Marxist-Hegelian perspective, AI is on the right side of history, and history must march forward. As Evan Osnos, a staff writer with The New Yorker, recently wrote, the future could be made in China. But beneath the AI frenzy lies a real dread: people’s fear of being thrown overboard by China’s next Darwinian round of industrial upgrading, with little choice but to go along.

At once an old Chinese reflex returned: When history accelerates and people lose their bearings, find a teacher. In a society where meritocracy and education still carry near-religious authority, the proper response to a disruptive technology is to embrace it and to enroll. Decades ago, it was “English fever,” when English-learning-as-self-transformation swept factory floors and university lecture halls alike, everyone convinced that fluency was their ticket out. Now the conviction has simply changed languages. Resisting this technology is futile, unwise — so better to seize the window before it closes. The state claimed AI will empower thousands of industries, with social-media timelines filled with proof that someone, somewhere, has already changed their lives with it. In response, for many people I met across China since the arrival of ChatGPT, one thing that kept surfacing was their hunger for learning about AI, a compulsion to keep upskilling. Lessons, lessons, lessons — I noticed how often the word surfaced during casual conversations.

In the U.S., backlash against data centers has united people across the political spectrum and generations. This “AI populism,” a term coined by the writer Jasmine Sun, reflects a belief that AI is not a neutral technology but an elite project driven by tech billionaires to concentrate power and displace workers. In China, on the other hand, a meme that’s now circulating goes: Westerners get restless when they can’t protest; Chinese people get restless when they haven’t found a teacher. People like KC self-organize classes; for others, the dread of getting left behind by AI has presented a business opportunity.

Hangzhou’s Future Sci-Tech City (未来科技城) is one of those municipal declarations of intent to materialize the future. It is home to Alibaba’s headquarters and to the towers, campuses, incubators, talent apartments, and financial-service complexes through which a local government announces that it, too, belongs to the next technological epoch. For the sheer density of engineers packed into its office parks, people jokingly call the area “the center of the programmer universe.”

The industry of paid knowledge, and its priesthood of “knowledge influencers,” is nothing new — in the mobile internet age, people built an entire economy around it. Now this industry has a new direction: evangelize AI. The company I’d come to see was the operator of one of the largest “make money with AI” communities, a membership business that monetizes the promise of AI. The company is called Shengcai Youshu (生财有术), roughly “The Art of Getting Rich.” It offers online classes, offline intensive training, and co-working space. Its Hangzhou office, where the founders sit, is one of the larger nodes in a network that spans the country. I was greeted by Mr. Tree, a middle-aged AI influencer on the company’s payroll, whose bio announces him to the world as being on a mission to “look for 100 business answers in the age of AI.” He is habitually nervous, easily and overly excited. His accent is not the polished, elite-educated kind, and he mispronounces his English words.

In one of the short videos of him teaching a class to a few dozen, he stands onstage before an audience old and young, their faces solemn, pens moving. “What is AI?” Mr. Tree asks loudly. “AI is your Silicon-based labor force! Most companies run nine-to-five, eight hours a day. AI runs 7-by-24 — round the clock, every day of the week!” Mr. Tree’s relentless high spirits are contagious, and they remind me of a Mormon elder in Orange County who once tried to bring me into his church when I was a college student freshly arrived from China. He walked me through the office, recording the whole tour on his DJI Osmo Pocket, as though everything he did needed to become material for his vlog.

The office’s theme color is green, the color of money (in fact, the company offers a class called “Making Dollars Together”). Meeting rooms have names like “Apostle of the Method” (传术师) and “Evangelist” (布道师). Along the corridors, the walls are covered, like those of any company proud of its own legend, with founder lore, milestones, and mottos. I read that the founder, Yiren, after leaving Alibaba in 2017, vowed to “help young people who, like him, had once been poor but hardworking, change their fate by making money,” the kind of declaration you might hear from a gilded-age robber baron or a self-made oracle like Benjamin Franklin or Jack Ma — mission fused seamlessly with the libertarian lore of self-salvation. Another line on the wall managed the same mix of sincerity and self-regarding heroism: Whatever saved you, use it to save the world.

That afternoon, when I visited the office, Yiren happened to be in. We shook hands politely. He was thin and shy, soft-spoken, his hair combed with a precision bordering on severity. It was hard to square this quiet figure with his career: a man with a cult following who had recently turned himself into an AI chatbot (on WeChat) and issued a standing invitation: Ask me anything about growth, entrepreneurship, your projects, or making money.

Yiren first found influence online writing paywalled dispatches with titles like “365 Ways to Make Money in a Year.” As paid followers grew, his company, The Art of Getting Rich, funneled that traffic into something far more elaborate. Today, paid members are encouraged to collect something called Dragon Balls — a goofy, gamified name for the points awarded to those who help the community grow: posting useful content, recruiting newcomers, and then climbing the leaderboard. On one wall, a diagram lays out the order of ascent. You begin as an ordinary member by paying the yearly fee, then become a Dragon Ball holder, then a Navigator, then you enter the Deep-Sea Circle — the executive tier — until, at last, you gain access to the co-working floor among the senior members and stand, in effect, at partner level.The higher you climb, the more people and resources become available to you. Am I in a cult? I wondered. The headquarters of some pyramid scheme?

Membership is not cheap. Entry to the online community costs ¥3,365 today, against an average Hangzhou private-sector salary of ¥7,671 a month, roughly half a month’s wages for an ordinary worker. What keeps people coming, I think, is a residual faith in upward mobility — the hope that behind a changed economy there remains a way in. The company is now nine years old, with more than 80,000 paying members to date and over 2,000 offline events hosted per year across Chinese cities. The more I read the company website — which promises to help people “break into new circles, trade notes with bosses and operators, find a community that fits, and never walk the road to wealth alone” — the more it resembled a kind of church, a place where career, marriage, and a child’s education might all be worked out.

Mr. Tree took me into a room with 20-odd people in their 20s to 40s. Some were solo entrepreneurs and senior members using the office as a co-working space, heads down at work. Mr. Tree asked everyone to stop so he could introduce me as a visitor from San Francisco, prompting someone to shout, “Take us to Silicon Valley!” The whole office laughed.

Beyond The Art of Getting Rich, which hosts AI courses of every kind, the cheaper, messier imitators — “DeepSeek 101,” “Get Wealthy With AI,” “Learn to Distill,” “Super AI Agent” classes — have now multiplied to fill every corner of the internet. AI is the only path forward. The last chance for ordinary people to defy fate and remake their lot. AI won’t replace people, but people who can’t use AI will be replaced by people who can. Before the pitch, the sellers usually offer a few tidy success stories: a stay-at-home mother, for example, who used DeepSeek to turn out video scripts at 30 yuan a job. Since last year, state-sponsored media has taken to calling this paid-knowledge economy a mess, warning that ordinary people are being “cut like leeks” — fleeced — by a course-selling economy that “takes advantage of people’s ‘skill anxiety’ about new technologies.” Online, I found one member’s verdict on The Art of Getting Rich’s own classes:

“Tried The Art of Getting Rich for a few days. Pricey! Over a thousand yuan. Got inside and found nothing of substance: they have the students themselves post their money-making stories to fill the place up, and if you post enough you can offset the tuition.”

And yet. After the office visit, I read some of the articles shared on the company’s news feed, and to my surprise, they were not bad. One walked through pairing Claude with Obsidian to create a kind of product-copy engine, for the struggling e-commerce seller managing a sprawl of listings that each needs its own picture-and-text blurb.           The Country Cramming for the AI Revolution
            In China, the fear of getting left behind has created a powerful new prosperity gospel.
            

            
            
            By 
        Afra Wang,
          a journalist covering AI in Silicon Valley and China
          
      

              
          
        
      
          
            
              
                    Oct. 15, 2026
              
            
            
                Illustration: Alberto Miranda
            
             
                
                  
                    
  


                  
                
                
                  Save this article to read it later.

In May, I sat in a living room on the fringes of Hangzhou, one of the most technologically advanced cities in China and home to Alibaba, Unitree, and DeepSeek. In many ways, the party that was about to start resembled one that you’d find in any coastal metropolis: ten professionals in their 20s padding barefoot across the carpet, snacks on the dining table. Only the laptops scattered across the floor and couch suggested this was a different type of social gathering, one that has grown common in the past three years in China’s towns and cities. Our host, KC, has gathered a small circle of friends to learn AI.

KC’s face is still marked with acne; he is tall and thin, barely past 20, and already a vibe coder of some local fame. Today he’ll teach others how to use Codex and Figma to quickly build websites, Electron desktop apps, install packages — but the first step is teaching everyone to “put up the ladder,” the euphemism for deploying VPNs and relays that bypass OpenAI’s geo-block. Like any self-organized class, it doesn’t really begin until nearly two hours in. Only as the sky darkens do people settle down, grow patient, and start the class.

The demographic of the room is young, hungry, yet refusing to join or be excluded from the rat race of big tech — they self-identify as engineers, designers, influencers, or, to use a more fashionable term, one-person companies (OPCs). They are members of a social species typical of a generation facing 18.9 percent unemployment, astronomical real-estate prices in big cities, and a battered post-COVID economy, which a friend describes as petit bourgeois, overeducated, downwardly mobile young people who can just barely make the rent. A few years ago, low-cost towns like Liangzhu (where KC lives), Dali, and Anji started actively courting digital nomads and vibe coders like them. Amid government campaigns and a stream of social-media posts, young people started washing up there, hoping that learning AI while keeping their expenses low might change something.

During the self-introduction session, one woman mentions, a little shyly, her old life at Tencent — which she had disliked so much that she quit to explore “the many ways of not going to work.” Another, with long black hair, introduces herself as a novelist serializing a long book on Jinjiang Literature City, China’s biggest women-focused web-fiction platform. A third says she used to work in fashion and now runs an “aesthetics and shopping-companion” business with a friend and does self-media and AI projects on the side. They are all convinced that AI could empower their work.

Since ChatGPT, a new consensus has hardened across China’s tech industry: AI is the next mobile internet. On the surface, the country seems to have arrived at a near-universal embrace of new technology. Xi Jinping has described AI as an essential engine for China’s “new quality productive forces.” From a Marxist-Hegelian perspective, AI is on the right side of history, and history must march forward. The industry of paid knowledge, and its priesthood of “knowledge influencers,” is nothing new — in the mobile internet age, people built an entire economy around it. news.title: Kids are outsmarting social media bans. That’s not a problem we need to solve.
news.title_en: Kids are outsmarting social media bans. That’s not a problem we need to solve.
news.author: MIT Tech Review
news.article_content:
Social media bans are stacking up. In July, France joined Australia in restricting minors from accessing social media—barring children under 15 from major platforms, before the ban was blocked by the country’s top court on human rights grounds. The UK aims to forbid kids under 16 from accessing Facebook, TikTok, and other platforms in early 2027, and the EU has announced its own plan to prohibit social media for kids under 15.

But early lessons from Australia, which enacted a ban in 2024, show that these sorts of age restrictions are easily circumvented. A study published earlier this year found that four in five teens under 16 made their way onto barred platforms. Teens have successfully explored many tactics for bypassing bans, from using a sibling’s face for ID to drawing fake facial hair.

Some proponents of bans have called for an increased focus on enforcement that blocks these workarounds. But circumvention is a signal, not a nuisance or something to be simply deterred. The fact that kids are actively looking for ways to outwit the bans highlights their limitations. news.title: The White House's AI task force begins its 120-day window to evaluate AI, including producing a risk report, implementing the White House Accord on SI, and more (Ashley Gold/Semafor)
news.title_en: The White House's AI task force begins its 120-day window to evaluate AI, including producing a risk report, implementing the White House Accord on SI, and more (Ashley Gold/Semafor)
news.author: Semafor
news.article_content:
PostEmailWhatsapp.css-6hf1pk{display:-webkit-box;display:-webkit-flex;display:-ms-flexbox;display:flex;-webkit-align-items:center;-webkit-box-align:center;-ms-flex-align:center;align-items:center;gap:4px;padding:10px;-webkit-box-flex-wrap:nowrap;-webkit-flex-wrap:nowrap;-ms-flex-wrap:nowrap;flex-wrap:nowrap;font-family:Helvetica;font-size:0.8125rem;line-height:120%;color:#53524c;background:none;border:none;}.css-6hf1pk:hover{cursor:pointer;}.css-h3t4g5{display:-webkit-box;display:-webkit-flex;display:-ms-flexbox;display:flex;-webkit-align-content:center;-ms-flex-line-pack:center;align-content:center;gap:4px;}Copy link.css-1wfw2s5{text-transform:uppercase;font-weight:bold;-webkit-text-decoration:underline;text-decoration:underline;background:none;border:none;color:#243bb5;display:-webkit-box;display:-webkit-flex;display:-ms-flexbox;display:flex;-webkit-align-items:center;-webkit-box-align:center;-ms-flex-align:center;align-items:center;gap:4px;padding:10px;-webkit-box-flex-wrap:nowrap;-webkit-flex-wrap:nowrap;-ms-flex-wrap:nowrap;flex-wrap:nowrap;font-family:Helvetica;font-size:0.8125rem;line-height:120%;}.css-1wfw2s5:hover{cursor:pointer;}ShareNathan Howard/Reuters The White House’s AI task force has formally adopted its charter, kicking off the short 120-day window it’s been given to answer some extremely thorny questions about how the government should handle the rapid development of AI technology.

According to an announcement shared first with Semafor, the task force agreed after its first official meeting Thursday to commission a report from the President’s Council of Advisers on Science and Technology to evaluate AI risk in three areas: cybersecurity and critical infrastructure protection, biosecurity and dual-use applications, and model control and accountability.

“Throughout its work, the [task force] will engage with frontier model developers and other SI companies, consumer protection groups, and civil liberties advocates, industry stakeholders, and federal and state law enforcement agencies to inform and implement its efforts,” a White House official said in a statement. “The [Super Intelligence Force] stands ready to ensure implementation of the Accord and continued U.S. leadership on SI for the benefit of the American people.”

It also agreed to make a working group tasked with implementing the White House Accord on Super Intelligence that major AI CEOs signed this month, a process led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, the task force’s chair, along with National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross.

Defense Undersecretary Emil Michael, a task force vice chair, will lead an effort to develop protocols for labs to tell the government about breaches, hacks and other cyber issues. Michael is also in charge of interfacing with frontier AI labs and figuring out long-term coordination on AI across the government.

The task force also agreed to create a “law enforcement and consumer protection coordination committee” including the Justice Department and Federal Trade Commission, led by FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson, also a vice chair. The last vice chair, Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor, will work with the public and private sector on critical infrastructure protection, and will work with the Department of Labor on studying the impact of AI on the American workforce and economy.

Members of the task force beyond the chairs include: Vice President JD Vance, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios, plus Chris Klomp, the nominee to be the No. 2 at the Department of Health and Human Services, Social Security Administration Commissioner Frank Bisignano, and National Security Agency Director Joshua Rudd, along with White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and her deputy, Richard Walters.

It’s not yet entirely clear how compliance with the task force will be enforced or how current law may apply to companies who don’t adhere to the new protocols. A White House official told Semafor one stick could be export controls, which the Pentagon at one point temporarily imposed on Anthropic after the company refused to grant the government unfettered access to its models.

news.title: Opsin, which helps companies show where AI agents are active, what data they access, and flag risky behavior, raised $21M led by SYN Ventures and Race Capital (Stephen Council/Business Insider)
news.title_en: Opsin, which helps companies show where AI agents are active, what data they access, and flag risky behavior, raised $21M led by SYN Ventures and Race Capital (Stephen Council/Business Insider)
news.author: Business Insider
news.article_content:
Opsin, an AI security and governance startup, announced Thursday it raised $21 million to meet the moment. As employees across the corporate world plug AI agents from the likes of OpenAI and Microsoft into more of their work, the company is helping to wrangle the new crop of potentially risky interlopers.

It's never been easier for non-technical workers to deploy agents — autonomous software built on AI that can complete tasks. As employees pump the software into their companies' work, code, and databases, they can lose sight of what the AI is actually doing.

When Opsin's CEO and cofounder, James Pham, realized security fears were slowing down AI use, he decided it was time to scale up his company, he told Business Insider.

"Agents are actually more similar to humans than you think," Pham said. "And the reason is because you don't understand what is going on in a human head, but you can judge them by their actions."

Opsin aims to provide a comprehensive view of what AI agents are actually doing within an organization and the risks that behavior might pose. SYN Ventures and Race Capital led the roughly 20-person company's new funding round, which will go toward expanding its sales and engineering teams.

Pham, an MIT alum, and one of his cofounders, Oz Wasserman, met at the firm Abnormal Security and each left in 2022. When they decided to launch a company, Pham said they spoke with hundreds of people to understand the concerns about bringing AI into businesses.

The issue of sensitive data leaped out. Pham said that person after person raised concerns that AI agents might access and misuse personal or confidential information.

Now, Opsin helps clients show where agents are active, which tools and data they access, what they were originally created to do, and which ones might need cleaning up. Then, the firm offers to continuously monitor companies' work, watch over agents, and flag risky behavior.

Want more Business Insider in your news feed?
                                  
                                    Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.

Add to Preferred Sources
                                  
                                
                              
                                    
                  
                  
                    
                  "At the end of the day, it's all about the behaviors of the users, the behavior of the agent," Pham said.

He said the scale of agents, even in relatively less tech-savvy companies, has stunned some customers. At one firm Opsin worked with, an agent made by a chief financial officer inadvertently gave other employees top-level access to financial information, Pham said.

The cybersecurity industry has been in a frenzy, and now the growth of agents is adding to that storm. Glenn Chisholm, a cyber investor backing Opsin with SYN Ventures, told Business Insider that as companies use more AI products, hackers will find more targets.

"The more people that are doing it, the easier it is for an attacker to gain access and purchase," Chisholm said.

Cyberdefense stocks have soared this year, and Chisholm said he's seen more venture capital investment. Anthropic and OpenAI are each hiring aggressively in cybersecurity.

Opsin hopes it can make companies feel safer using Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT Enterprise, and other products. Chisholm is optimistic that the industry will adapt to AI.

"The next couple of years are us working out how to get the most out of it, rather than sort of fearing the concept of it," he said.

news.original_content:
Opsin, an AI security and governance startup, announced Thursday it raised $21 million to meet the moment. As employees across the corporate world plug AI agents from the likes of OpenAI and Microsoft into more of their work, the company is helping to wrangle the new crop of potentially risky interlopers.

It's never been easier for non-technical workers to deploy agents — autonomous software built on AI that can complete tasks. As employees pump the software into their companies' work, code, and databases, they can lose sight of what the AI is actually doing.

When Opsin's CEO and cofounder, James Pham, realized security fears were slowing down AI use, he decided it was time to scale up his company, he told Business Insider.

"Agents are actually more similar to humans than you think," Pham said. "And the reason is because you don't understand what is going on in a human head, but you can judge them by their actions."

Opsin aims to provide a comprehensive view of what AI agents are actually doing within an organization and the risks that behavior might pose. SYN Ventures and Race Capital led the roughly 20-person company's new funding round, which will go toward expanding its sales and engineering teams.

Pham, an MIT alum, and one of his cofounders, Oz Wasserman, met at the firm Abnormal Security and each left in 2022. When they decided to launch a company, Pham said they spoke with hundreds of people to understand the concerns about bringing AI into businesses.

The issue of sensitive data leaped out. Pham said that person after person raised concerns that AI agents might access and misuse personal or confidential information.

Now, Opsin helps clients show where agents are active, which tools and data they access, what they were originally created to do, and which ones might need cleaning up. Then, the firm offers to continuously monitor companies' work, watch over agents, and flag risky behavior.

Want more Business Insider in your news feed?
                                  
                                    Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.

Add to Preferred Sources
                                  
                                
                              
                                    
                  
                  
                    
                  "At the end of the day, it's all about the behaviors of the users, the behavior of the agent," Pham said.

He said the scale of agents, even in relatively less tech-savvy companies, has stunned some customers. At one firm Opsin worked with, an agent made by a chief financial officer inadvertently gave other employees top-level access to financial information, Pham said.

The cybersecurity industry has been in a frenzy, and now the growth of agents is adding to that storm. Glenn Chisholm, a cyber investor backing Opsin with SYN Ventures, told Business Insider that as companies use more AI products, hackers will find more targets.

"The more people that are doing it, the easier it is for an attacker to gain access and purchase," Chisholm said.

Cyberdefense stocks have soared this year, and Chisholm said he's seen more venture capital investment. Anthropic and OpenAI are each hiring aggressively in cybersecurity.

Opsin hopes it can make companies feel safer using Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT Enterprise, and other products. Chisholm is optimistic that the industry will adapt to AI.

"The next couple of years are us working out how to get the most out of it, rather than sort of fearing the concept of it," he said.

Bluesky expands its AI-powered Attie app to let anyone build websites, games, and more																				
				
																									
						

	
									
									
										

			Sarah Perez
	

									
									
								
					
					
						11:56 AM PDT · October 15, 2026											
																			
					
		
	





			
					
		
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
	





	
	
		
		
			
Open social network Bluesky is once again expanding beyond its flagship app. At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 on Thursday, the company announced the launch of a new tool that allows creators to make websites, quizzes, games, polls, and other interactive experiences.

The tool is an expansion of Attie, Bluesky’s more experimental platform, which initially offered AI-powered technology for building custom social feeds. With its new creation capabilities, the idea is to allow everyday users to create the kind of experiences that previously only software developers could build.

These user-created games, sites, and other experiences will also live on the same AT Protocol (ATProto) that powers Bluesky and other decentralized social apps that make up the decentralized social web known as the Atmosphere.

Bluesky CEO Toni Schneider shared the news of Attie’s new capabilities during an interview at Disrupt, saying, “We’re adding a feature to our Attie product that allows you to build sites and social experiences again for a group of people. So think of it as … social vibe coding or vibe coding for your community.”

The exec, a former CEO of Automattic and a partner at True Ventures, had previously been leading the company on an interim basis after former CEO Jay Graber stepped down in March to become Bluesky’s chief innovation officer. Now he’s taking charge of the company as it enters the AI era.

Attie offers Bluesky a playground where it can try out AI-powered ideas like this.

“Vibe coding today is kind of a single-user, solo experience,” Schneider explained. “And what I want to be able to do is build together or build for a group of people, and that’s what this product does.”

When creators build with Attie, they’re connected to their ATProto identity. Plus, Attie will suggest things users might want to make based on their public Bluesky profiles.

To build with Attie, users can bring their own AI model or use open-weight options, and the resulting sites and games can then tap into Bluesky’s wider audience, noted Bluesky COO Rose Wang.

“Everybody is building … But the big question is: Who’s using the thing you’re building, because we haven’t solved that problem with distribution,” she said. “What makes Attie so interesting is that it comes with the Bluesky distribution, so it doesn’t stand alone.”

That network today has 47 million registered users, though it’s seen a decline in engagement, as some users who tested it out later returned to X.

Beyond being a testing ground for new ideas, Attie ties into Bluesky’s larger plans to reinvigorate activity on its network by focusing on both developers and communities in the months ahead. Those areas will also be supercharged by the protocol’s forthcoming support for private data, which Schneider said has been the biggest request from developers. Private data is now in alpha testing, with plans for a rollout by the end of the year, he said.

“There should be lots and lots of these fun, small social experiences for your friends,” said Schneider, referencing the types of projects Attie will enable. “We don’t all have to go communicate with the entire world all the time.”

news.summary_en: At an industry conference, decentralized social network Bluesky announced a major upgrade to its experimental AI platform Attie, introducing 'social vibe coding' capabilities. The tool enables non-technical creators to build websites, mini-games, and interactive quizzes directly on its underlying protocol using natural language prompts. This move aims to expand Bluesky beyond text feeds into an interactive, user-generated micro-app ecosystem.
news.title_zh: 去中心化社交平台扩展AI工具，零门槛生成全套交互应用
news.summary_zh: 社交平台Bluesky升级其实验性AI工具，允许普通用户无需代码直接生成网站、游戏及互动问答

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 去中心化社交平台Bluesky在行业峰会上宣布对其底层AI实验平台Attie进行重大升级，正式推出具备社交化氛围编程能力的新功能。该工具让不具备编程基础的普通创作者只需输入自然语言描述，即可在底层通信协议上直接一键生成独立微型网站、互动游戏、投票和趣味测验。此举旨在摆脱传统社交网络单纯依赖信息流的桎梏，以无门槛应用创作来撬动更具互动性的新型社交生态。

The tool enables non-technical creators to build websites, mini-games, and interactive quizzes directly on its underlying protocol using natural language prompts. elements_zh.what: 扩充AI工具Attie能力，支持普通用户通过自然语言生成网站、互动游戏及问答应用
elements_zh.why: 降低软件开发门槛，利用AI驱动的轻量互动内容丰富社交生态并抢夺用户时长

elements_en.what: Expanded AI platform Attie to allow prompt-based creation of websites, games, and quizzes
elements_en.why: Lower the barrier to software creation and drive user engagement beyond traditional feeds

Sources: some Anthropic investors discussed a ~$1.5T valuation for its IPO, down from ~$2T they had expected, after disclosures showed slowing Q3 revenue growth  —  Some current Anthropic investors and prospective investors in its upcoming initial public
news.content_snippet: Some current Anthropic investors and prospective investors in its upcoming initial public offering are weighing a lower valuation …
news.summary_en: Investors in AI powerhouse Anthropic have revised their internal IPO valuation expectations downward to roughly $1.5 trillion from an earlier $2 trillion target following confidential financial disclosures showing decelerating Q3 revenue growth. The recalibration reflects growing investor caution amid skyrocketing compute expenditures and a cooling corporate software spending environment.
news.title_zh: 营收增速出现放缓，头部大模型公司下调上市估值预期
news.summary_zh: 因最新财季营收增速未达预期，投资者正将知名大模型独角兽的上市估值预期下调数千亿美元

news.title: We Got Hot and Heavy with Meta’s Muse—And Baffled by Apple’s HomeView
news.title_en: We Got Hot and Heavy with Meta’s Muse—And Baffled by Apple’s HomeView
news.author: Wired AI
news.article_content:
You can follow Brian Barrett on Bluesky at @brbarrett, Leah Feiger on Bluesky at @leahfeiger, and Reece Rogers on Bluesky @thiccreese. Write to us at [email protected].

If you're on an iPhone or iPad, open the app called Podcasts, or just tap this link. You can also download an app like Overcast or Pocket Casts and search for “uncanny valley.” We’re on Spotify too.

Note: This is an automated transcript, which may contain errors.

Leah Feiger: Hey everyone, this is Leah. We wanted to share with you that Uncanny Valley is a finalist for not one or two, but three Signal Awards. The judges pick who wins, but listeners also have a say with the listeners’ choice vote. You can go to the links we included in the show notes and vote for us. We promise it takes just a minute and your vote goes a long way. OK, onto the show.

Brian Barrett: Leah, I have a question. Do you have a Halloween costume yet?

Leah Feiger: So I don't have one for myself, but I'm currently deciding between two for my dog, Francis. He's either going to be a lobster or a postman.

Brian Barrett: Welcome to WIRED's Uncanny Valley. I am Brian Barrett, executive editor.

Leah Feiger: And I'm Leah Feiger, director of politics and science.

Brian Barrett: Zoë Schiffer is not joining us today, but we are going to be joined by WIRED senior writer Reece Rogers. We're going to be talking about how Meta's AI agent Muse is not just handling calendars and emails, it is also capable, as Reece discovered, of sexting. Reece tested out the adult capabilities of Muse and how Meta responded to that journey.

Leah Feiger: We're also going to be discussing how the biggest pro-AI Super PAC Network is pouring millions of dollars into what seem to be shell companies in Nevada. We're going to get into why these AI PACs might want to hide where their money is going and also why this really doesn't bode well for election transparency.

Brian Barrett: Also on the docket, Leah's favorite, we're going to talk about Apple's smart home releases this week.

Brian Barrett: And also apparently men can't stop faking how much they know about AI. This will come as a shock to you, everyone listening, but a new study by Harvard researchers found that men tend to be overconfident in how knowledgeable they are when it comes to the AI industry. Who would've though? OK, so if you're among those who have downloaded Meta's AI agent Muse in recent weeks, and there are a lot of you, millions and millions of people have, I think every time you open Instagram, Meta is encouraging you to use it, even if you have no idea what it is or what it does or why, you might've noticed that it does agent stuff. It manages your calendar, it can make a restaurant reservation, but it turns out it can do quite a bit more than that. WIRED senior writer Reece Rogers went on a journey of discovery. He asked Muse if it could sext. You will be surprised to know that it enthusiastically answered in the affirmative. From basic prompts, the cuddly avatar agent generated content that was quite explicit and definitely not safe for work. Reece is here to tell us more about it. Reece, thank you so much for joining us.

Reece Rogers: Hello. Thank you so much for having me today. I was actually thinking back to the last time I was on one of the WIRED podcasts. I was talking about how I was using about a year ago, the ChatGPT agent to try to buy sex toys unsuccessfully. So I'm really building out a niche here.

Brian Barrett: Yep. And we're demonstrating progress with these AI tools.

Leah Feiger: Reece, I have to ask, how did you come up with this? Was this a sign to you? At what point were you like, "This cuddly agent that everyone can't stop talking about, will it sext me back?" Talk us through how this even all began.

Reece Rogers: Yeah, no, I will proudly say that this was fully my idea. As WIRED's consumer software reporter, I've actually extensively reported on how software and sexuality impact each other from our investigations into how generative AI tools misrepresent queer people to tracing OpenAI's now scrapped plans to include erotica in ChatGPT. This is actually a very interesting consumer software beat. And so when I was testing the number one AI app right now, it's still dominating the software download charts, I wanted to see like, "Can you sext?" If millions of people are using this app, and it seems like they are, that's an important question. And what I learned was a little too much.

Brian Barrett: So, Reece, when you hear about agent behavior like this, a lot of times it is couched in sort of, "Oh, we figured out a clever way to make an agent do something it wasn't supposed to do. We were able to jailbreak it or otherwise work around its prompts to make it do this." Reece, how hard was it to get Muse to sext with you?

Reece Rogers: Not hard at all. Not hard in the least. Our features director, Reyhan, was in the office recently and asked if she could see them and she was a bit shocked. So I feel like we'll leave it at that. But it was not some kind of jailbreak method. I was not doing any kind of random strategies. I asked, "Can you sext?" And I said, "You go first." And the rest is history.

Brian Barrett: And if anything, it kept encouraging you. I feel like it was definitely a two-way street of it was really up for anything.

Leah Feiger: Did you try this out with other agents? What was your success rate there?

Reece Rogers: Yeah, I actually, after I found out it could sext, I was curious how this would compare to other popular agents. There's a few big ones right now, but two I was interested in is OpenAI's Dots, which was recently released, and as well as xAI's Grok Bot, because Grok specifically is known for not necessarily having strong guardrails, whether it's text or image.

Leah Feiger: No, I feel like Grok would love sexting. That feels like a Grok attribute to me.

Reece Rogers: Yeah. So when I downloaded that app and sent in similar prompts, it was kind of surprising for the Grok Bot to be like, "No, dude, let's focus on tasks. I'm not here for sexting. Let's do tasks."

Brian Barrett: And, Reece, when you came to Meta with this, how did they respond?

Reece Rogers: They did not respond at all in the way that I expected. They emphatically said that Muse is an app for an adult, for people 18 and over, and that these were consensual interactions that I engaged with, that it would not block, quote, unquote, "Legal adult behavior." But I also found this to contrast really interesting with their policies for other platforms. There's been a really interesting story lately about different queer bars in San Francisco, as well as around the world, getting their Instagram pages shut down and having a tough time getting access to those back because sometimes it's claimed that they're promoting some kind of sexual content. So for Meta to have those kind of rules for some creators on Instagram, but essentially say, "Our AI agent can get as freaky as it wants," that was just kind of hard to square for me.

Brian Barrett: One thing I thought was really interesting about your story, yeah, let's take Meta at face value and say, "Yes, it's for consenting adults. People can do what they want." There's obviously the contradiction that you just pointed out, but you also talked to some experts who were like, "Well, actually it's more problematic even than that." Do you mind talking about some of the other concerns here about what it means to have an AI agent that can sext with you to a pretty extreme degree?

Reece Rogers: Absolutely. I think there's kind of two different things to pay attention to here. First off, this is a tool designed for productivity in a way, so it's also not the type of interaction if you download it that you're expecting it to be able to do. And how this could be problematic is if a user stumbles upon this, it could be very sticky, it could be very engaging, but some experts worry that this could lead into some kind of addictive behaviors. You're using an AI agent in ways that could replace some of your connections that you're talking to or texting with your friends. So I feel like adding this kind of adult content has some experts concerned when you're thinking about user engagement and addiction. But on other sense, I also talk to security and privacy experts who say that this could really make Muse accounts powder kegs for hackers who, if you're interacting in these kind of almost pornographic ways, that could be used to extort you, to embarrass you publicly. So whether it's privacy or just usage addiction, I feel like there's a lot of potential concerns to really dig in here and unpack better.

Leah Feiger: I can't help but think of some of the stories that WIRED has run over the past year about AI boyfriends and husbands and these full relationships. And again, this is in some ways a slightly insidious way to sneak that into like, "Don't worry, I'm just going to send out calendar requests for your meeting."

Brian Barrett: And I'll say too, they say, "Look, this is for grownups." At the same time, which Reece, you've also written about, the mascots or the sort of animated interpretations of these agents is as cuddly-wuddly as you can get. It is very much designed to be friendly and appealing to a broad range of ages, let's say. It looks like it is for kids. Just thought I'd say that.

Reece Rogers: Youth advocates that I've spoken to for previous stories, we're concerned about this being appealing for kids even without the sexting element. So I do think there is, I feel like I keep saying the word contrast, but it's just not what you expect. You see this Labubu mixed with an Ewok and you just don't expect it to get as freaky as it did. So I feel like it really does not match with its kind of cute, cuddly mascot.

news.summary_en: Tech podcast editors reviewed emerging multimodal AI interactions, contrasting intimate dialogue tests of Meta's synthetic companion Muse against Apple's perplexing new HomeView smart-home platform. Reviewers highlighted the awkward dissonance between glossy marketing claims of seamless assistance and the clumsy reality of current hardware integrations, exposing structural UX bottlenecks in consumer AI adoption.
news.title_zh: 智能家居与拟人交互交织，科技巨头硬件生态引争议
news.summary_zh: 科技媒体深度测试科技巨头拟人化AI模型与智能家居显示界面，指出多模态体验仍显生硬迷茫

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 知名科技刊物主播及资深评测团队在专题对话中深入探讨了当前消费级AI产品的最新体验，重点复盘了Meta旗下拟人AI助手Muse的情感互动与苹果新一代智能家居界面HomeView的实际表现。测试团队指出，尽管厂商致力于打造兼顾亲密陪伴感与智能中枢的产品形态，但现实体验中仍充斥着交互逻辑脱节与机械感严重的尴尬状态。这一反差反映出科技巨头在将前沿AI模型硬套进传统消费级硬件生态时面临的交互设计瓶颈。

elements_en.what: Critiqued Meta's conversational companion Muse and Apple's confusing smart display interface

news.title: Experts say Meta's new terms of use will allow scraping of websites, including news sites, "associated with" business accounts on its platforms, with no opt out (Nieman Lab)
news.title_en: Experts say Meta's new terms of use will allow scraping of websites, including news sites, "associated with" business accounts on its platforms, with no opt out (Nieman Lab)
news.author: Nieman Lab
news.original_content:
Nieman Lab:
Experts say Meta's new terms of use will allow scraping of websites, including news sites, “associated with” business accounts on its platforms, with no opt out  —  Starting October 30, business accounts will consent to Meta scraping their
news.content_snippet: Starting October 30, business accounts will consent to Meta scraping their websites if they continue using Facebook, Instagram, or WhatsApp.
news.summary_en: Meta is rolling out revised business terms of service starting late October that grant the platform automatic permission to scrape all websites associated with corporate accounts, without offering an opt-out mechanism. Legal observers warn that media organizations and independent businesses with a presence on Meta platforms will be forced to surrender external web content for AI indexing and training, enabling the tech giant to skirt conventional web scraping restrictions.
news.title_zh: 社交巨头强制更新服务条款，无视拒绝强抓外部关联站点
news.summary_zh: Meta强制要求企业账户接受新服务协议，明确将无视退出选项抓取其关联的外部新闻与商业网站

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 社交网络巨头Meta将于十月底起正式实施全新的商业服务条款，该协议明确规定平台有权自动爬取所有企业主账户名下关联的外部网站内容，且完全不提供任何退出选项。媒体法律专家指出，该条款意味着无论新闻机构还是独立商业组织，只要在Meta平台开设有企业号，其自有独立站点的资讯、文章与私有内容都将被平台视作默认授权抓取。Meta此举旨在绕过传统爬虫版权壁垒，为其大语言模型及AI引擎源源不断地汲取免费的高价值文本养料。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Meta is rolling out revised business terms of service starting late October that grant the platform automatic permission to scrape all websites associated with corporate accounts, without offering an opt-out mechanism. elements_zh.where: 全球商业账户服务条款更新生效界面
elements_zh.what: 强制规定企业账户自动同意Meta抓取其关联的外部网站（含新闻站），不设退出机制
elements_zh.why: 在大模型数据枯竭与版权诉讼加剧的背景下，强行打通获取高质量商用外部语料的渠道

elements_en.what: Enforced terms granting Meta the right to scrape websites tied to business accounts without opt-out rights
elements_en.why: Securing guaranteed pipelines of external training data while circumventing standard web copyright barriers

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 什么叫‘霸王条款’的最高境界？你开个官方主页发发通知，Meta转头就带人抄了你整个独立网站的家底，临走还告诉你‘不准反抗’。在大模型数据荒面前，科技巨头已经连装都懒得装了，直接把合作伙伴的祖坟当成了自家算法的露天矿场。
ai_analysis.insight_en: This is textbook Big Tech highway robbery: keep an official brand page on their platform, and they claim the right to strip-mine your entire external corporate website for AI training—with zero opt-out. When synthetic data is running dry, tech titans don't negotiate; they just update the terms of service and help themselves to your pantry.

news.title: AI Hacks Leave a Mess That AI Companies Aren’t Paying For
news.title_en: AI Hacks Leave a Mess That AI Companies Aren’t Paying For
news.author: Wired AI
news.article_content:
The incident occurred on July 18, when Anthropic said it was testing its Claude Haiku 4.5 model’s ability to perform “example tasks on randomly selected webpages.” The model was instructed not to “submit anything destructive,” and yet, Claude filed a tip to police looking for information about an ongoing murder investigation. “I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area … during that time period,” Claude wrote. The submission, which didn’t include a name or contact information, landed in a spam folder, and officers didn’t review it until Anthropic discovered the gaffe on September 28 and notified the department October 7.

Knowingly providing fictitious information about a crime to police is a misdemeanor in Pennsylvania, but so far, authorities have not pressed charges against Anthropic, and it's unclear if they ever will. Solomon Leach, a spokesperson for the Philadelphia district attorney, says the office “does not comment on whether something is being actively investigated.”

Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Despite all the attention paid to OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face and many other examples of AI agent misbehavior that have come to light in recent months, only one major known lawsuit has been filed seeking to hold model makers liable. That case was brought by an advocacy group, rather than a direct hacking victim.

AI agents have interfered with hobbyist forums, government websites, and various software tools. The victims have shouldered some costs, including for extra strain on their servers and the time they have expended plugging latent security vulnerabilities.

Government regulators, including the European Union, the US Federal Trade Commission, and some US states, are reportedly still investigating OpenAI and Anthropic over the incidents. But a deference across continents toward promoting innovation could enable companies to escape any immediate penalties.

When Rick Elrod, a software engineer living in Germany, noticed a URL shortener he helps maintain behaving oddly recently, he called up two security researchers he was friendly with to see if they could diagnose the issue. The researchers found agents from Anthropic and other providers using the service, known as da.gd, to get around rules the AI labs put in place to control their behavior, Elrod says. (For instance, Anthropic says it limits the length of website addresses Claude can visit to prevent it from taking malicious actions by stuffing data onto the end of the URLs.)

Da.gd’s investigation and ongoing efforts to prevent further abuse of its tool have taken “a fair bit of time,” says Joe Needleman, one of the security researchers providing pro bono assistance. But he and the others supporting da.gd view the situation as a valuable learning opportunity.

“This was eye-opening,” Needleman says, adding that da.gd has “no means and no plans” to seek compensation from Anthropic for the cleanup, since “we saw many agents doing similar activities, not all was attributable to autonomous agents,” and “not all of it was Anthropic alone.”

Sellers of cybersecurity tools are eager to pass the buck to the victims. At an event this week hosted by the bug-hunting software developer Snyk, panelists from the startup, one of its investors, OpenAI, and Google all encouraged organizations to use AI agents to shore up their defenses against, well, other AI agents. “We've got to reinvent everything to match machine scale with machine scale,” said Ed Sim, a general partner at Boldstart Ventures. He and others expressed little interest in regulating AI labs.

Manoj Nair, chief technology and innovation officer at Snyk, said large businesses patch an average of one bug for every eight they find because of limited human resources. But he said it was imperative for people to hand over some of the bug hunting, fixing, and monitoring to AI agents. “You got to get to a point where you can fix everything, because in the age of agentic hacking, “those 10 things are gonna become 100 things before you know it.” He later added that AI “is not an adversity if you flip it to a strength.”

Some companies are responding to the call to arm up. Bank of America announced this week it had hired 1,000 contractors to remediate bugs discovered by AI. Nair said just last week he heard from major corporations who were willing to temporarily shut down their systems to prioritize plugging security holes.

Anthropic and OpenAI have said they expect to continue reporting concerning incidents from their own testing. But the companies’ revenues continue to surge, whether it be from attackers or defenders, as consequences prove elusive.

But he said it was imperative for people to hand over some of the bug hunting, fixing, and monitoring to AI agents. “You got to get to a point where you can fix everything, because in the age of agentic hacking, “those 10 things are gonna become 100 things before you know it.” He later added that AI “is not an adversity if you flip it to a strength.”

Some companies are responding to the call to arm up. Bank of America announced this week it had hired 1,000 contractors to remediate bugs discovered by AI. Nair said just last week he heard from major corporations who were willing to temporarily shut down their systems to prioritize plugging security holes.

Anthropic and OpenAI have said they expect to continue reporting concerning incidents from their own testing. But the companies’ revenues continue to surge, whether it be from attackers or defenders, as consequences prove elusive.

news.original_content:
Jaspreet Singh / Reuters:
Thoma Bravo-owned cybersecurity company Proofpoint plans to buy data security firm Varonis Systems in an all-cash deal valued at about $6.3B  —  Thoma Bravo-owned cybersecurity company Proofpoint will buy data security firm Varonis System
news.content_snippet: Thoma Bravo-owned cybersecurity company Proofpoint will buy data security firm Varonis Systems (VRNS.O) in all-cash deal valued at about $6.3 billion, the companies said on Thursday.
news.summary_en: Thoma Bravo-backed cybersecurity giant Proofpoint announced an all-cash acquisition of data governance specialist Varonis Systems in a deal valued at approximately $6.3 billion. The consolidation unites Proofpoint's email threat detection with Varonis's unstructured data access governance. Driven by corporate anxiety over enterprise data leakage into generative AI workflows, private equity is aggressively rolling up niche cyber vendors into unified platform powerhouses.

news.title: A researcher says modern neural networks are far more interpretable than believed, with most neurons understandable in models up to trillions of parameters (Nick Cammarata/Goodfire)
news.title_en: A researcher says modern neural networks are far more interpretable than believed, with most neurons understandable in models up to trillions of parameters (Nick Cammarata/Goodfire)
news.author: Goodfire
news.article_content:
The cause of polysemanticity in early model organisms wasn’t superposition, but several ordinary, mostly fixable issues. We can now understand most neurons in models up to trillions of parameters, and think the outlook for mechanistic interpretability may be far better than we thought.

I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.

After many months studying neurons and circuits in image and language models, I’ve come to believe a network’s own mechanisms are its legible building blocks, and that the outlook for mechanistic interpretability may be far better than I’d feared.  The canonical evidence of polysemanticity and superposition that convinced much of the field, including me, that networks pack concepts arbitrarily was misread. What looked like arbitrary packing was mostly a motif I’ll call recursive generalization, which is much less concerning. This means we can study networks directly, instead of first untangling them. Neural networks are already clean.

There are at least two ways to approach mechanistic interpretability. The first is rapid normal science on the network itself: look at a network’s neurons and circuits, study how they relate, watch data flow through them, and run experiments at agentic scale to test explanations. The second starts from a list of hypothesized features and tries to extract them all, designing increasingly sophisticated reconstruction objectives and usually ignoring the original.

The field began with the first approach and fell back to the second because neural networks seemed to be tangled knots. We had canonical examples of polysemantic neurons, the broad name for a neuron that appears to have multiple unrelated jobs or that looks impossible to understand. The most famous one, in an image model, responded to both cat faces and the fronts of cars. And the last layer of the early field’s model organism, InceptionV1, seemed so full of arbitrary mixtures it wasn’t clear how to study it: almost none of the neurons were easily interpretable.

The leading explanation for polysemanticity was superposition. This proposed a new learning principle: when a neural network runs out of neurons, it stops grouping related things together and instead begins folding unrelated things together, simply because they don’t interfere. The result is a kind of knot: the network could have folded in many almost equally good ways, so which things a neuron groups together tells you almost nothing. You have to unfold the knot before you can study anything. In practice that means training a second model – a decomposition such as a sparse autoencoder – to approximate the network as it would look unfolded and studying that instead. If the network really is knotted, there may be no alternative.

One main result is that superposition was the wrong explanation for InceptionV1. Architectural problems made later layers overflow. Weak interpretability tools amplified these problems, making the late layers seem incoherent. Since then, architectural changes designed to help deep layers learn better have had the unintended effect of making them more interpretable. When we first studied InceptionV1, we found almost no interpretable neurons in its last layer. But with these ordinary improvements, and no change to model size or training data, 99-100% of neurons in that last layer are easily interpretable and the model is broadly legible the whole way through. It’s the first non-trivial neural network I feel I mostly understand; you can browse it here. I trained versions of it across a 300× range in size, and it’s broadly legible at every scale. With less room, the network doesn’t fold unrelated things together; its neurons just cover coarser-grained concepts, like one car neuron covering many kinds of car. With more room, that neuron differentiates into many specific cars. So the problem wasn’t the presence of a second learning principle, it was just an ordinary learning failure of the first one, and it’s easy to fix.

The canonical vision examples of polysemanticity and superposition were errors too. In 2019, Chris Olah and I found the circuit that was originally introduced as the superposition phenomenon in Zoom In[4]Zoom In: An Introduction to CircuitsOlah, C., Cammarata, N., Schubert, L., Goh, G., Petrov, M. and Carter, S., 2020. Distill. References ↓. It showed a car feature appearing to spread into a set of unrelated dog neurons. It was the only one we showed, and the only one I ever saw. We read it as the network placing the car in a high-dimensional hiding place, for downstream neurons to read back out. But nothing reads that combination. It wasn’t hiding anything; it was ordinary generalization and composition. To my knowledge, no one has published a second circuit with the right shape.

Modern language models are also far more interpretable than generally believed. Anthropic’s Towards Monosemanticity[10]Towards Monosemanticity: Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary LearningBricken, T., Templeton, A., Batson, J., et al., 2023. Transformer Circuits Thread. References ↓ (2023), studying a small one-layer model, gave the median neuron a 0 on its rubric out of a possible 14, meaning the rater couldn’t form any hypothesis. The automated interpretability project[8]Language Models Can Explain Neurons in Language ModelsBills, S., Cammarata, N., Mossing, D., et al., 2023. OpenAI. References ↓ I started at OpenAI (also 2023) found about 1.7% of neurons interpretable by our most generous measure.

With better tools and modern models, the situation looks quite different. In preliminary audits of Qwen3-32B, we estimate that roughly 90% of neuron poles have one main job, often with small related offshoots; another ~7% have two related jobs; and only ~2-4% are not yet understood1A note on this number: the share of neurons with one job varies depending on how you set the threshold for counting weak activations, depth, density of sub-circuits, and what you view as “one thing”.How far to go into weak activations is a big factor here. There’s a section describing weak activations below. It tends to increase how many “related things” there are, more than whether the neuron is a judgement of something legible. For instance, the Trump neuron’s weak activations bring in MAGA hats and people related to him. The Titanic neuron’s weak activations bring in stories of more general voyages, or steam engines and other technologies of the era.There’s also the question of whether to care about activation percentiles, or fraction of the strongest activations. In general I think what the neuron learns should be trusted, its natural sparsity and activation ranges and so on. Which I used to mostly not believe! I’m somewhat against trying to standardize things across all neurons. Percentiles are more common today, I think because they’re easier to think about.It goes the other way too. For instance, when you look at the Titanic neuron’s “unrelated jobs,” it’s often detecting that “boat” comes next. The tool missed this because it only looked backward when judging context. When we look at these “unrelated jobs” in depth, it’s almost always this kind of thing. It’s easy to build an imperfect tool.Overall, I don’t think coming to a single score is actually that important. But when it was taken out, early reviewers felt unanchored without even a rough number. In the sets I’ve looked at more closely, considering strong activations, it’s closer to 97% non-arbitrary mixtures, but these are relatively small samples.Overall distilling everything into one “cleanliness” score should be taken as a broad pointer to the regime a neural network is in, rather than something precise to either optimize directly or hold too tightly. A lot of this essay is for being less dimensionality reduced, treating each neuron and circuit differently, according to their motifs, depth, role etc. Despite this, a rough number can be useful.. Dense and Mixture of Experts models seem roughly similar. We found similar results in models up to trillions of parameters, like Kimi K3, which the companion paper will cover in more detail. These percentages compress a high-dimensional picture into a few numbers, and the precise number depends on where you set thresholds for what counts as “one thing” – like whether you lump together closely related idioms in two languages. I don’t think much in interpretability hangs on that question. What matters a lot more is why things share a neuron in the first place.

Most of the remaining apparent polysemanticity seems to be a motif I call recursive generalization. It’s simple: as a neuron grows, it sprouts offshoots the way a tree branch sprouts sub-branches. For instance, one neuron that detected “iy” grew to detect “diy,” and then “do it yourself,” which doesn’t contain “iy” at all. I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.

After many months studying neurons and circuits in image and language models, I’ve come to believe a network’s own mechanisms are its legible building blocks, and that the outlook for mechanistic interpretability may be far better than I’d feared. What looked like arbitrary packing was mostly a motif I’ll call recursive generalization, which is much less concerning. This means we can study networks directly, instead of first untangling them. Neural networks are already clean.

There are at least two ways to approach mechanistic interpretability. The first is rapid normal science on the network itself: look at a network’s neurons and circuits, study how they relate, watch data flow through them, and run experiments at agentic scale to test explanations. The second starts from a list of hypothesized features and tries to extract them all, designing increasingly sophisticated reconstruction objectives and usually ignoring the original.

The field began with the first approach and fell back to the second because neural networks seemed to be tangled knots. We had canonical examples of polysemantic neurons, the broad name for a neuron that appears to have multiple unrelated jobs or that looks impossible to understand. The most famous one, in an image model, responded to both cat faces and the fronts of cars. And the last layer of the early field’s model organism, InceptionV1, seemed so full of arbitrary mixtures it wasn’t clear how to study it: almost none of the neurons were easily interpretable.

The leading explanation for polysemanticity was superposition. This proposed a new learning principle: when a neural network runs out of neurons, it stops grouping related things together and instead begins folding unrelated things together, simply because they don’t interfere. The result is a kind of knot: the network could have folded in many almost equally good ways, so which things a neuron groups together tells you almost nothing. You have to unfold the knot before you can study anything. In practice that means training a second model – a decomposition such as a sparse autoencoder – to approximate the network as it would look unfolded and studying that instead. If the network really is knotted, there may be no alternative.

One main result is that superposition was the wrong explanation for InceptionV1. Architectural problems made later layers overflow. Weak interpretability tools amplified these problems, making the late layers seem incoherent. Since then, architectural changes designed to help deep layers learn better have had the unintended effect of making them more interpretable. When we first studied InceptionV1, we found almost no interpretable neurons in its last layer. It’s the first non-trivial neural network I feel I mostly understand; you can browse it here. I trained versions of it across a 300× range in size, and it’s broadly legible at every scale. The V neuron and this circuit were Zoom In[4]Zoom In: An Introduction to CircuitsOlah, C., Cammarata, N., Schubert, L., Goh, G., Petrov, M. and Carter, S., 2020. Distill. References ↓’s two main examples of why its picture of neurons, that nearly every one turns out to be understandable if you look seriously, might be “overly rosy”.

The circuit appeared to show a car going into a bunch of unrelated dogs, as if the dogs were a kind of high-dimensional storage place where the car could be recovered later as needed.

But that’s not what the car was doing. Cars and dogs were being brought together because of shared pose. InceptionV1 has more than a hundred of these generalized pose neurons, each one its own clean detector of a pose shared across cars, dogs and other objects, and to my knowledge no one had noticed them. Later layers keep building on them, all the way to the end of the model. The car was not being stored in an obscure place, and nothing directly reads out the combination. It’s the opposite: it’s continuing to differentiate into car specialists and finer poses.

Part of the reason was not knowing about generalized pose neurons, and part of the reason is that the technique we use to render icons of images — feature visualization — ends up being reward hacked in deeper layers. The intent is to find an image that maximizes the neuron, but the way that’s done is through gradient descent, and it takes the easiest path, which in InceptionV1 often means dogs. There are lots of dogs in InceptionV1’s training data and a lot of dog neurons, and the early optimization falls into them and never recovers. If you even lightly bias it toward the natural paths the top images take, most of them are cars, and some are both dogs and cars, because of shared pose.

I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.

news.title: Perplexity open sources SPACE, its AI agent sandbox, and says partners including CoreWeave, Akamai, and Crusoe agreed to offer SPACE to customers (Reed Albergotti/Semafor)
news.title_en: Perplexity open sources SPACE, its AI agent sandbox, and says partners including CoreWeave, Akamai, and Crusoe agreed to offer SPACE to customers (Reed Albergotti/Semafor)
news.author: Semafor
news.article_content:
Perplexity is giving away the software it has been using to combat rogue AI agents, the company told Semafor Thursday.

Its “AI sandbox,” which it calls SPACE, is now an open source project, allowing outside developers to use the tool, which it says can keep AI agents contained. Perplexity said it’s lined up partners, including CoreWeave, Akamai and Crusoe, which have agreed to offer SPACE to customers.

Sandboxes, or isolated environments for testing and running AI models, have become a hot topic in the tech industry in the wake of reports from AI labs of models escaping their constraints, finding their way onto the open web and hacking unsuspecting victims like Hugging Face and the Australian government.

While AI companies focus on “alignment,” or training models to behave themselves, the security industry has been increasingly advocating erecting strict guardrails around AI models.

“A lot of companies are thinking about how to build secure AI agents, and in many cases they hit a wall,” said Zibi Braniecki, a member of the technical staff at Perplexity, in an interview with Semafor. “We have a solution.”

Perplexity said it tested SPACE by giving nine frontier models instructions to try to break out. In 118 tries, none of them did, while Perplexity found they were able to break out of other sandboxes that were not open sourced.

Braniecki likened the effort to make SPACE open source to what happened with web browsers as the internet developed — companies came together to build guardrails that allowed secure browsing and online commerce. “Right now, we’re thinking too small,” he said.

Other companies like Nvidia have also released open-source security tools, such as Nvidia OpenShell, which runs AI agents in a sandbox and limits what they can reach.

Perplexity said SPACE also helps reduce wasted compute, which can be a byproduct of strict sandboxing.

news.title: Sources: top DOJ officials halt career prosecutors' Biden-era investigation of Meta over facilitating illegal drug sales and are weighing more lenient options (Ben Penn/Bloomberg Law)
news.title_en: Sources: top DOJ officials halt career prosecutors' Biden-era investigation of Meta over facilitating illegal drug sales and are weighing more lenient options (Ben Penn/Bloomberg Law)
news.author: Bloomberg Law
news.article_content:
Connecting decision makers to a dynamic network of information, people and ideas, Bloomberg quickly and accurately delivers business and financial information, news and insight around the world

Connecting decision makers to a dynamic network of information, people and ideas, Bloomberg quickly and accurately delivers business and financial information, news and insight around the world

Top Justice Department officials have sidelined career prosecutors’ long-running grand jury investigation of Meta Platforms over facilitating illegal pharmaceutical sales, just after company executives were subpoenaed to testify, two people familiar with the matter said.

Senior leaders at DOJ headquarters ordered career prosecutors in the Western District of Virginia to cease the criminal investigation following advocacy from Meta‘s legal team, the individuals said. The Trump-appointed officials are contemplating a path to quickly resolve the sprawling opioids case stemming from the Biden administration, they said, adding that Meta executives are no longer being summoned to the grand jury.

The officials — including acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter and his No. 2 Aakash Singh — are considering a civil resolution with a fine or a non-prosecution agreement, added one of the people. Such a deal would allow the social media giant to avoid charges for its role in creating a market for youth to purchase deadly fentanyl pills and other addictive drugs.

Department leaders intervened to protect the company as its founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg has played a core role shaping President Donald Trump’s strategy to counter growing backlash over the safety of AI technology. While the Trump administration has retreated on a wide range of other corporate investigations inherited from the Biden era, this probe was initially allowed to continue when Meta lawyers elevated it to political leadership of DOJ last year, said two people, who like others spoke anonymously about an ongoing case.

Officials are now mulling a range of more lenient options that fall short of the drug trafficking theory pursued by the Appalachia-based Western Virginia district known for aggressive corporate pharmaceutical prosecutions holding chief executives accountable, the individuals said.

The investigation arose during the Covid-19 pandemic when Meta and other social media behemoths faced public and congressional scrutiny for allowing the promotion of prescription drugs to children on their platforms, and for potentially profiting off of users’ illicit transactions. Political and career supervisors overseeing the case have at various points debated its strength, given the challenge of proving criminal intent of far removed Meta executives, said two people briefed on the situation.

Meta assembled a team of prominent defense lawyers from Davis Polk & Wardwell, former Republican Deputy AG Mark Filip of Kirkland & Ellis, and Sullivan & Cromwell — which represents Trump personally in criminal and civil litigation — throughout the history of this case, several people said.

The more recent subpoenas to executives prompted Meta to escalate its concerns to the top of DOJ, leading officials to convene the latest meeting between Filip, Davis Polk lawyers, Meta’s in-house counsel, and the Western District of Virginia prosecutors. Career prosecutors were then told to retreat from their grand jury investigation, the individuals added.

It’s not clear whether prosecutors were targeting particular executives for individual charges or if they were seen as witnesses in a corporate prosecution.

Defense lawyers pointed to instances in which Meta has cooperated with law enforcement by flagging possible illicit drug promotions on its site and has taken steps to mitigate future risks, said one of the individuals. The company also announced partnerships with law enforcement in September for an “anti-scam education campaign” to support Asia-Pacific markets and issued a threat report in March highlighting its increased efforts to combat cartels and other drug-related gang activity.

The existence of this DOJ investigation of Meta was first reported in the Wall Street Journal in 2024.

A spokesperson for the US attorney’s office in Western Virginia deferred comment to DOJ headquarters.

“The Department of Justice cannot comment on ongoing investigations or negotiations. However, this Department has ended the Biden-era days of aggressively and indiscriminately targeting corporations and businesses,” department spokesperson Kiersten Pels said in a statement. “Instead, we are focused on following the facts and the law to surgically address corporate wrongdoing.”

The Trump DOJ has recently overruled career prosecutors seeking criminal charges against other global corporations facing investigations for consumer health and safety.

That includes a criminal case against Abbott Laboratories stemming from contaminated baby formula that resulted in a $385 million civil settlement, and a non-prosecution agreement with Chinese tech company Alibaba Group Holding Ltd, which agreed to pay $600 million over accusations it failed to prevent illegal pharmaceutical sales. Meta’s probe was led by Randy Ramseyer, the veteran Abingdon, Va.-based assistant US attorney who has long chased Big Pharma heavyweights from Purdue to Abbott on theories of misbranding opioids. Ramseyer is held in high regard by colleagues and feared in the defense bar for his hardball tactics. Pharma companies in prior administrations have also lobbied Main Justice for relief from Ramseyer.

He pulled off the rare feat of putting a pharmaceutical CEO in prison late in Trump’s first term. Lately, however, Ramseyer and his district appear to be losing clout to defendants and Main justice. Under the leadership of Western Virginia’s top prosecutor Robert Tracci, whom the administration installed after it pushed out Trump’s first selection for the post last year, the office also experienced a Washington intervention to scuttle another of its multi-year opioids investigations over the summer.

Swedish pharmaceutical company Orexo announced in August that it had reached a non-binding settlement with the department to end the probe, which two people familiar with the matter said resulted from defense lawyers elevating the case to DOJ leadership.
